text: Last lesson traced one invoice through the XLA tables as part of a bigger journey. This lesson slows down and looks at those tables on their own terms, because Subledger Accounting isn't a Payables feature or an AR feature — it's one shared engine every subledger routes through.

Before architectures like this existed, each subledger could write its own logic for turning transactions into GL entries. Oracle Fusion centralizes that in Subledger Accounting, sometimes called the Financials Accounting Hub. Payables, Receivables, Fixed Assets — all route through the exact same engine and the exact same core tables.

The core tables, precisely: XLA_TRANSACTION_ENTITIES identifies the transaction generically. XLA_EVENTS records each accounting event tied to it. XLA_AE_HEADERS and XLA_AE_LINES are the subledger journal entry itself. XLA_DISTRIBUTION_LINKS ties a journal line back to its exact source distribution.

SLA doesn't invent debits and credits out of nowhere. Each ledger has configured accounting rules — mapping logic saying, for this kind of event, debit this account and credit that one. That's why the same kind of transaction can post differently for two companies on the same instance, if their ledgers have different rules configured. The engine is shared; the configuration isn't.

Centralizing this logic means every subledger gets the same auditability for free: trace a journal line back through distribution links, through events, to the original transaction, no matter which subledger it started in. Chapter four is complete. Up next, chapter five: using everything you've learned so far in practice.
